kicker: Qwen4-Max, read against its own sources

steps.say: Sixteen panels, six models, and the new one in bold blue on every one of them.
Alibaba's Qwen4-Max launched today. No weights, no report. A paragraph, a diagram, a price list, and this chart.

scenes.headline: How Qwen4-Max spends 2.4 trillion parameters
scenes.sub: The architecture, the benchmark rows, and the bill
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Thatch. Let's read the machine first, then check every bar, then work out the bill.

scenes.title: Active per token, billions
scenes.say: The total is the same as the last flagship, two point four trillion. What changed is how much each token touches: seventy-one billion, down from ninety-five. A quarter less compute per token.

steps.say: And the machine is new. Three linear-attention layers, then one sparse-attention layer, repeated up the stack.
steps.term: GDN: Gated DeltaNet, a fixed-size memory

steps.say: Inside each layer, four residual lanes, read and written through gates.
And at layer two, a lookup table keyed on short runs of tokens. It is the same drawing Qwen published for Flash-Next in August.

params.ctx: a long context, one row of micro-blocks
params.full: full attention compares with every token
params.gdn: Gated DeltaNet folds history into a fixed state
params.idx: the indexer scores blocks, not tokens
params.sel: QSA attends inside the best blocks only

steps.say: Here is the problem. Full attention compares every new token with every old one, and keeps them all. At a million tokens that is the whole cost.
Three layers in four fold the history into a fixed-size state instead. Cheap, constant, and lossy: a summary cannot always find one exact clause.
So the fourth layer goes back to the real tokens. A light indexer scores micro-blocks of four tokens, which makes the choosing itself cheaper.
Then it attends only inside the best blocks. Past the budget, the only part still growing with context is that cheap scan.
Follow one token up the stack.

steps.term: N-gram embedding: a lookup by recent tokens
steps.say: At layer two it picks up a vector from a three hundred and twenty-eight billion parameter table. A lookup, not a multiply, so it can live in host memory.
Three cheap memory layers, one sparse attention layer.
Then the experts, seventy-one billion of them active.
Everything passes through four gated lanes instead of one stream.

steps.caption: no axis for tokens or steps
steps.say: It trained cleanly at that scale. But the curve has no token count, and there is no word on data or the R L recipe.

scenes.title: Checking the bars
scenes.sub: Every comparator against someone else's number

states.say: Sixteen panels, with the new model in bold in every one.
It has the highest bar in four. In the rest, usually Opus is ahead. It beats its own predecessor everywhere.

steps.caption: Opus 59.6 here, 66.4 on Anthropic's page
steps.say: Terminal-Bench is the odd row. Anthropic's own page puts Opus seven points higher than this.
Every bar in this panel is Artificial Analysis's run, to the decimal. A fair source. The footnotes just do not say so.

scenes.title: Where each panel's numbers come from

states.say: Checked against rival cards and public leaderboards, panel by panel.
Seven match a named source. Two are Artificial Analysis's without a footnote. ProgramBench has two bars that differ from Moonshot's card. Six I could not check.

scenes.title: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index
scenes.say: On a neutral index it lands below all four rivals, including the open Kimi. Strong on document work, weak at terminal coding, and the least likely of them to invent an answer.

scenes.title: The bill
scenes.sub: Cheapest list price, not always the cheapest task

steps.say: At the same effort it uses about half the tokens on Terminal-Bench, for a higher score.
These are output tokens. At four fifty a million, they cannot add up to the claimed cost per task. Most of the bill is cached input.

scenes.title: Where the cut per task comes from

steps.say: Qwen says a Work360 task cost four forty-three on the old model.
Charge the same tokens at the new prices and it is already about two fifty. Most of the saving is the price list.
Fewer tokens take it the rest of the way, to one sixty-seven.

scenes.credit: video from Qwen's post on X

steps.caption: 475 minutes to 24, marked Pending Confirmation
steps.say: The case studies deserve the same care. This table claims ninety-five percent, and prints pending confirmation under its own result.

scenes.credit: video from Qwen's post on X

steps.say: And the coolant run said to work entirely on its own has a person at hour nineteen, holding up a sample that changed colour and steering the next round.

scenes.text: A hybrid architecture that trains cleanly at 2.4T, at the lowest list price on its chart. Measure your own cost per task.
scenes.mark: Measure your own cost per task
scenes.say: A hybrid design that scales cleanly, a mostly honest chart, and the cheapest list price on it. But it is verbose, so measure your own cost per task.

recap: Three memory layers per sparse-attention layer
Seven panels match a source, two are unlabelled
Cheap per token, verbose per task
scenes.say: Fixed memory plus sparse attention, a chart checked bar by bar, and a bill that depends on tokens. Thanks for watching!
